_about: English for the dictionary's hand-written definitions and origin stories, keyed by the Spanish text. Other definitions follow the pattern «Se usa en … para decir …», written in English by the app.

definitions.Interjección para llamar la atención de: An interjection to get someone's attention or to address a friend. Used all the time in Argentina and Uruguay.
definitions.Forma uruguaya de llamar a alguien con c: The Uruguayan way to call someone you know well, much like the Argentine «che».
A mess, a commotion or a chaotic situation.
A kid or a young person. For a girl, «piba».
definitions.Persona lenta, tímida, ingenua o tonta;: A slow, shy, naive or foolish person; the one who stands watching the party without joining in.
definitions.«A la brigandina» sugiere que algo se hi: «A la brigandina» means something was done in a hurry and carelessly, with poor results.
definitions.Hecho con prisa, sin cuidado y, por lo t: Done in a rush, without care, and so done badly.
definitions.Autobús. Ojo: en Argentina, Chile y otro: Bus. Careful: in Argentina, Chile and other Andean countries «guagua» means baby.
definitions.Forma coloquial de llamar al colectivo o: A casual word for the colectivo, the bus.
definitions.Banana o plátano dulce que se come crudo: A sweet banana, eaten raw. In Venezuela «plátano» is the one you cook.
definitions.Palomitas de maíz. Se dice sobre todo en: Popcorn. Said mostly in Santo Domingo; in the southwest of the country it's called «gallitos».

origins.Origen incierto. Mucha gente cree que vi: Uncertain origin. Many people believe it comes from the English «pal», but that isn't documented.
origins.Viene del kimbundu «kilombo», que nombra: From the Kimbundu «kilombo», the name for settlements of people who escaped slavery in Brazil. In the River Plate it came to mean first a brothel and then any kind of mess.
origins.Se usa en el Río de la Plata desde final: Used in the River Plate since the late 19th century. The most accepted explanation is the Genoese «pivetto», 'boy', brought by Italian immigrants; another links it to «pebete».
origins.Del náhuatl «itzcuintli», 'perro'. Prime: From the Nahuatl «itzcuintli», 'dog'. It first named the Mexican hairless dog (the xoloitzcuintle) and then, jokingly, children.
origins.Origen incierto. Se suele relacionar con: Uncertain origin. It's often linked to the English «chum» ('friend'), but that isn't documented.
origins.No se sabe con certeza. La explicación m: Nobody knows for sure. The most cited explanation is African: it would come from Efik, a language of Calabar (in today's Nigeria), brought to Cuba by enslaved people and later spread around the Caribbean. Other theories, like the Chevrolet car, don't hold up.
origins.Del inglés «heavy», adaptado a la pronun: From the English «heavy», adapted to Dominican pronunciation.
origins.Según la historia popular, viene del ing: According to popular history, it comes from the English «party watcher»: during the US occupation (1916–1924), Dominicans called that the soldiers who watched the parties without dancing.
origins.La palabra «brigandina» se deriva de «Br: The word «brigandina» comes from «Bridge and Dinna», an American company that built bridges in the Dominican Republic under the dictatorship of Rafael Leonidas Trujillo. They became known for doing poor, careless work on those bridges.
origins.Del italiano «lavoro». Entró al lunfardo: From the Italian «lavoro». It entered the lunfardo of Buenos Aires with Italian immigration at the end of the 19th century.
From the Italian «lavoro». It entered the lunfardo of Buenos Aires and Montevideo with Italian immigration at the end of the 19th century.
origins.Se suele contar que nació con los bracer: It's often said to have started with the Mexican braceros who went to work in the United States in the 1940s, but the word was already used in Mexico to mean 'work' in the late 19th century. Its origin is still unsolved.
origins.Del nombre comercial Birome, formado con: From the brand name Birome, made from the surnames of László Biró, the Hungarian inventor who settled in Argentina, and his partner Juan Jorge Meyne. The pen went on sale in Buenos Aires in the mid-1940s.
origins.Su origen se discute. La explicación más: Its origin is debated. The most cited explanation is the English «wagon». The word was used in Cuba before it reached the Canary Islands, where it appears in the early 20th century.
origins.Del portugués de Brasil «bonde» (tranvía: From the Brazilian Portuguese «bonde» (tram). According to popular history, Rio's trams were financed with bonds, and the name passed to the vehicles.
origins.Se suele explicar porque los primeros ba: Usually explained by the first bananas reaching the Caribbean from the coast of Guinea, in Africa.
origins.Origen incierto. La historia de que vien: Uncertain origin. The story that it comes from the English «corn to fry» is popular but has no support: «cotufa» already existed in Spain's Spanish for a tuber, and it's also used in the Canary Islands.
origins.Diminutivo de «cancha», del quechua «kam: A diminutive of «cancha», from the Quechua «kamcha», 'toasted corn'.
origins.Del guaraní «naná», a través del portugu: From the Guarani «naná», through the Portuguese «ananás».
origins.Del náhuatl «popotl», el tallo hueco de: From the Nahuatl «popotl», the hollow stem of a plant, which was used as a straw.
origins.Probablemente del inglés, aunque no se s: Probably from English, though nobody knows which word: «safety can» and «save a can», the slogan on World War II recycling bins, have been proposed. Neither is proven.
origins.Del quechua «wawa», 'niño pequeño, bebé': From the Quechua «wawa», 'small child, baby'. It has nothing to do with the Caribbean guagua (bus): they're two different words spelled the same.
origins.Del quechua «puchu», 'sobra, resto': pri: From the Quechua «puchu», 'leftover, remainder': first the cigarette butt, then the cigarette.
origins.Del náhuatl «élotl», 'mazorca tierna de: From the Nahuatl «élotl», 'tender ear of corn'.
